blocks.text: He describes the house sparrow, البيوتي [al-buyūtī] domesticum, thus:- في طباعه اختلاف وذلك فيه من الطباعه ما يشبه السباع وهو اكله اللحم ولا يزق فراخه ومن البهايم انه ليس بذي مخلب ولا منسر وياكل الحب والبقول وهو اذا سقط علي العود قدم اصابعه الثلاث واخر الدايرة وساير الطير تقدم اصبعين وتوخر اصبعين وتميز الذكر منها بلحيه سودا كما الرجل والتيس والديك وليس في الارض طاير ولا سبع ولا بهيمة احني من العصفور علي [II, 725] ولده ولا اشد له عشقا ^{a)} وذلك مشاهد عند اخذ فراخه ووكره في الغمران تحت السقوف خوف من الجوارح واذا حلت مدينة من اهلها ذهبت العصافير منها فاذا عاد واعادت العصافير والعصفور لا يعرف المشي وانما يثب وثبا وهو كثير السفاد فربما سفد في الساعة الواحدة ماية مرة ولذلك قصر عمره فانه لا يعيش في الغالب اكثر من سنة والفرخه تدرب علي [col. 149] الطيران حتي انه يدعي فيجيب قال الجاحظ انه رجع من فرسخ It is of a combative nature. For something wild has been implanted in it by nature. Accordingly it eats meat, and does not feed its young by inserting its beak into their mouths. But it has this in common with birds that are not birds of prey: it has no talons with which to tear, nor a hooked beak, and it eats grain and vegetables. When it alights on a tree, it extends three of its four toes forward and one backward, whereas in other birds two toes are in front and as many behind. The male is distinguished from the female by a black beard, which it has like a man, a he-goat, or a cock. Nowhere is there a bird, wild beast, or beast of burden more devoted to its offspring, or that loves it more ardently. Hence it places its young and its nest in inhabited places, and under the roofs of houses, for fear of birds of prey. When a city is deserted, the sparrows leave it, and return together with the inhabitants. The sparrow does not know how to walk, and moves only by hopping. It is a bird so given to coition that it sometimes mates a hundred times in an hour, and consequently it is short-lived and usually does not live beyond a year. Its young are more teachable than the common run of birds, so that when called they respond. That the sparrow returns from a distance of a parasang is attested by Algiahid. One might add more to these from Alkazuinius, but things that suit the whole genus of sparrows, not the house sparrow alone.

In Hebrew צפצף tsiphseph means to murmur and to mutter, Es. VIII, 19. and XXIX, 4. This is taken from the chattering of birds. R. Selomo on Es. XXIX.: ציפצוף הוא לשון קול לחש כקול עופות דקין, Tsiphtsuph signifies a muttering voice, like the voice of little birds. This is clear from Es. XXXVIII, 14., where it is applied to the swallow. Yet more properly צפצוף is the chirping of sparrows. Pomarius: צפצף עשה קול צפורים, Tsiphseph, he chirped in the manner of sparrows. That this is true is clear from the Arabs, for whom صغصف [ṣaghṣaf] tsophtsoph is عصفور [ʿuṣfūr] sparrow, and صغصفة [ṣaghṣafa] tsaphtsapha is صوته [ṣawtuhu] its voice. So it is found in Alcamus. Hence it is that in Es. [II, 726] X, 14. the Hebrew words ופצה פה ומצפצף, And opening the mouth, and chirping, are rendered in Greek thus: Καὶ ἀνοίγων στόμα, καὶ στρουθίζων [Kai anoigōn stoma, kai strouthizōn]. On which Theodoret says: Ἀπὸ τῆς κρατούσης συνηθείας παρὰ ἀνθρώποις εἴρηται τῇ γραφῇ. εἰώθαμεν γὰρ λέγειν περὶ τῶν λίαν ἀγωνιώντων, Οὐκ ἐτόλμησε γρύξαι· οἱ δὲ λοιποί φασιν, Οὐκ ἐτόλμησε τρύσαι. τὸ οὖν Ἀνοίγων στόμα, καὶ στρουθίζων, ἀντὶ τοῦ Οὐ μόνον οὐδεὶς ἀντιπαρατάξασθαί μοι τολμήσει, ἀλλ᾽ οὐδὲ γρύζειν στρουθοῖς παραπλησίως ἐπιχειρήσει. [Apo tēs kratousēs synētheias para anthrōpois eirētai tē graphē. eiōthamen gar legein peri tōn lian agōniōntōn, Ouk etolmēse gryxai; hoi de loipoi phasin, Ouk etolmēse trysai. to oun Anoigōn stoma, kai strouthizōn, anti tou Ou monon oudeis antiparataxasthai moi tolmēsei, all' oude gryzein strouthois paraplēsiōs epicheirēsei.] This was adopted by Scripture from human usage. For we are accustomed to say of those who are in great straits, He did not dare to mutter. Others say, He did not dare to squeak. So 'opening the mouth and chirping' (there will be no one) is the same as if he said: Not only will no one dare to oppose me, but no one will even attempt to chirp like sparrows. From the same source comes that entry of Suidas: Στρουθίζων· τρίζων [Strouthizōn: trizōn]. For τρίζειν [trizein], to squeak, is also said of sparrows, as is clear from Iliad 2, line 314, where the serpent devoured the eight little sparrows with their mother
